subject: Banking
title: What Is a Credit Score?
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: What Is a Credit Score?.

hook.text: A three-digit number decides if you get a home, a car, or a credit card. Your credit score controls your financial life.

buildup.text: Credit scores range from 300 to 850. Above 740 is excellent. Below 580 means most lenders will say no.

discovery.text: The score predicts the probability you'll miss a payment in the next 24 months. Higher score means lower risk.

twist.text: 30% of credit reports contain errors. A mistake you don't know about could be silently lowering your score right now.

climax.text: A single number summarizes your entire financial history.

punchline.text: 300 to 850. One number controls your access to credit.

quiz.question: What does a credit score predict?
options: The probability you'll miss a payment in the next 24 months

details.summary: A credit score is a three-digit number between 300 and 850 that represents a statistical prediction of how likely you are to repay borrowed money. Lenders use it as a quick assessment of credit risk when deciding whether and at what rate to lend.
details.whyItMatters: Your credit score affects your ability to get a mortgage, car loan, credit card, apartment, and even a job. This single number influences some of the most important financial decisions in modern life for billions of people worldwide.
takeaways: Scores range from 300 to 850, with higher meaning lower risk
The score predicts the probability of 90-day delinquency within two years
Different lenders may use different scoring models and have different cutoffs

faq.question: What credit score do you need for a mortgage?
faq.answer: Conventional loans typically require 620 or higher. FHA loans accept 580 with 3.5 percent down or 500 with 10 percent down. The best interest rates are reserved for scores above 760. Each lender has its own specific thresholds.

faq.question: Does checking your own credit score lower it?
faq.answer: No. Checking your own score is a soft inquiry that does not affect it. Only hard inquiries from credit applications lower your score, and even those typically drop it by only 5 to 10 points temporarily.
